title: Spin-valley-layer coupling with dual control via stacking and electric field in antiferromagnetic bilayer Janus YIBr
abstract: The modification and enhancement of antiferromagnetic two-dimensional semiconductor is considered crucial for realizing novel electronic properties and facilitating promising applications. For this purpose, we investigate six antiferromagnetic 2D bilayer Janus YIBr structures with different stacking variations by means of first-principles calculation and an effective low-energy model. The calculation of magnetic anisotropy energy shows that the direction of easy axis varies with different stacking. First-principles-calculated energy bands reveal that there is a Dirac relativistic dispersion relation in the valence band in a wide energy window of 0.3 eV at least. The calculations for spin, atom properties and Berry curvature description show that there is spin, valley and layer coupling with spin splitting, valley polarization and quantum valley Hall insulators can be achieved in the bilayer Janus structures. Further analyses of the effect of external electric field can be used to control spin, valley and layer of the hole near the Fermi level. These can be useful in future exploration for novel properties, control methods and more functionalities in bilayer Janus structures.
summary: This theoretical study explores the tunability of spin-valley-layer coupling in antiferromagnetic bilayer Janus YIBr materials. By combining different stacking arrangements with an applied electric field, researchers demonstrate a mechanism to control quantum properties like valley polarization and induce Dirac-like dispersion relations. This work suggests the material's potential for advanced electronic applications such as novel filters or memory elements.
main_problem: The study investigates how spin, valley, and layer degrees of freedom can be coupled and controlled using stacking variations and external electric fields in antiferromagnetic bilayer Janus YIBr structures.
main_result: The system exhibits tunable spin-valley coupling, leading to potential quantum valley Hall effects, which can be continuously modulated by combining structural changes (stacking) with an applied electric field.
method: The research employs first-principles Density Functional Theory calculations combined with the development and fitting of effective low-energy Hamiltonian models.
model_or_system: The physical system is an antiferromagnetic 2D bilayer Janus YIBr structure, analyzed across six different stacking configurations. The theoretical framework involves modeling spin, valley, and layer coupling using generalized Hamiltonians incorporating external electric field terms.
key_observables: Spin splitting (up to $\sim 0.4 	ext{ eV}$), valley polarization ($\pm 0.08 	ext{ eV}$), Berry curvature distribution, and magnetic anisotropy energy.
important_parameters: External electric field strength ($E$), stacking configuration type (AA vs AB), and the resulting easy axis direction (in-plane vs out-of-plane).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on DFT calculations using GGA+U approximations, and the low-energy physics is modeled by fitting parameters ($\alpha,  eta$) to the calculated valence band structures.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate band structures showing spin splitting and valley polarization for different stacking types (AA1, AB3) under varying easy axis conditions. Berry curvature maps confirm the Quantum Valley Hall effect in certain configurations, and later figures show electric field control over these properties.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by first establishing the magnetic ground state via MAE calculations across six structures. It then analyzes band structure features (spin/valley splitting) dependent on stacking and easy axis direction. Finally, it models the system using effective Hamiltonians to demonstrate how external electric fields provide an additional continuous control knob for these coupled quantum properties.
why_interesting: The ability to engineer multiple degrees of freedom (spin, valley, layer) simultaneously via structural design and external fields is highly relevant for designing next-generation spintronic or topological memory devices that go beyond simple charge transport.
